To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
high intake of dairy products is associated with lower risk of diabetes in Australian men.
dairy foods are associated with a reduced incidence of diabetes among men in the Australian population.

high intakes of total dairy food, low-fat dairy food, high-fat dairy food and milk were all independently associated with a lower risk of developing diabetes, and that this was particularly true for men, although the results were not significant in women.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a lack of evidence that the consumption of dairy foods is associated with a reduction in the risk of developing diabetes.
there is no evidence to support a protective association of dairy foods and diabetes risk.
dairy food intake does not reduce the risk of developing diabetes in adults.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dairy foods do not reduce the risk of developing diabetes.
dairy foods, especially milk, may be beneficial for reducing the risk of developing diabetes.
dairy foods are not associated with diabetes, but there is a suggestion that dairy food intake may reduce the risk in men.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dairy foods, particularly milk, may have a protective effect against the development of diabetes.
dairy foods may reduce the risk for diabetes in men, but the evidence is not strong enough to recommend that men should eat more dairy foods for this reason.
dairy foods are an important source of nutrients in the Australian diet and should not be avoided by people with diabetes.
